blocks.title: AI & Me
blocks.description: Find the AI already in your day, distinguish it from fixed-rule software, and start asking who it helps and who it might harm.
blocks.mission: Create a one-page AI in My Day map showing at least five systems that use AI. For two of them, show INPUT → AI ACTION → OUTPUT → BENEFIT → RISK.
route: Experience Lab: draw for the AI
blocks.final: Draw-for-the-AI lab evidence, AI in My Day map, human-vs-AI comparison, and exit reflection.

sessions.title: AI or not?
sessions.intro: Vote before you get a definition, then use three questions to revisit your first instinct.

study.title: Three questions that help
body: There is no perfect one-line test for AI. A useful starting point is to ask whether a system uses data, finds or generates patterns, and adapts or predicts rather than only following one fixed rule.
Automation is not automatically AI. A timer and a calculator can be useful software while still following explicit rules written by people.
Modern products can mix ordinary software and AI, so some examples are genuinely borderline. Your job is to explain the evidence for your choice, not to force everything into one box.
study.example: A timer follows a fixed setting. A spam filter can use patterns from earlier examples to estimate whether a new message is spam.

activity.title: Hook: AI or not?
activity.instructions: Choose AI, not AI, or unsure for each. You can change your answers after reading the study material.

sessions.reflection: Choose one example and explain what evidence makes you think it contains AI, rather than only a fixed rule.

sessions.title: Can AI recognise what I draw?
sessions.intro: Predict what an AI will do, watch what it actually does, then change your input and see what changes.

study.title: Recognition is pattern-matching, not understanding
body: A recognition system compares your input with patterns learned from millions of earlier examples. It does not know what a cat is; it knows what most people's cat drawings looked like.
That is why it can guess a rough sketch in seconds and still fail on an unusual, tilted or partial drawing. The failure tells you what the training data looked like.
A good experiment records the prediction before the result, the result itself, one failure, and what changed when the input changed.
study.example: Draw a bicycle with two circles and a bar and the AI may guess it instantly. Draw the same bicycle from the front and it may say 'glasses'.

sessions.title: AI in My Day
sessions.intro: Map a normal day and make the hidden input-to-output chain visible.

study.title: The influence lens
body: To understand an AI system, follow the chain: INPUT is the data that goes in; AI ACTION is the pattern-finding, ranking, prediction or generation; OUTPUT is what comes out.
Then ask about consequence. BENEFIT asks who gains. RISK asks what could go wrong. A final stakeholder question is: who might be affected besides you?
Recommendation systems can create feedback loops: what you click today can influence what you see tomorrow, which can influence what you click next.
study.example: Listening history → finds patterns in what similar people play → playlist → new music discovery → risk of repeatedly hearing more of the same.

activity.instructions: Add five systems from waking up to going to sleep. Complete the full chain for at least two rows.

sessions.reflection: Which system on your map has the most influence over you, and who else could be affected by its output?

sessions.title: Human vs AI
sessions.intro: Compare strengths without assuming either humans or AI are automatically better.

study.title: Ability is not the same as responsibility
body: Current AI systems can be fast at pattern-heavy tasks, generating alternatives, sorting large amounts of information and producing fluent output.
Humans bring lived context, values, responsibility, judgement about consequences and the ability to decide when a task should not be automated.
A useful comparison asks not only who can do a task, but who should make the final decision and who is accountable when something goes wrong.
study.example: A recommendation model can rank thousands of songs quickly. A person can decide whether the recommendation is appropriate for a particular situation and can reject it.

sessions.title: Exit reflection
sessions.intro: Finish Chapter 1 by putting the idea into your own words.

study.title: Myth-busters to remember
body: AI does not simply mean robots; most AI you meet is software such as ranking, filtering, prediction or generation.
Not every computer program is AI. Fixed-rule software and learned systems can exist side by side.
Using AI does not make a system objective. Data and design choices come from people and can still produce unfair outcomes.
study.example: A system can be consistent every time and still be consistently unfair.

blocks.title: Teaching a Machine
blocks.description: Teach a computer to tell two objects apart, then deliberately find where it fails and improve it with evidence.
blocks.mission: Train a two-class model, produce a 10-row test log and confusion matrix, find one failure pattern, improve the model, and show before-and-after evidence.

sessions.title: Be the classifier
sessions.intro: Try written rules first so you can see why machine learning uses labelled examples.

study.title: From rules to learning
body: Supervised learning teaches a model with examples that already have the right class label attached.
A feature is something measurable about an example, such as shape, edges, brightness or proportions. The model learns statistical patterns in those features; nobody types every rule into it.
Training data are the labelled examples used for learning. Test data must be genuinely different, otherwise you are mostly testing memory rather than generalisation.
study.example: Instead of writing ‘cups have handles’, show the model many labelled cup and bottle examples and let it learn separating patterns.

sessions.title: Build model v1
sessions.intro: Collect balanced, varied examples and record the conditions before you train.

study.title: Training data shapes the model
body: A balanced dataset contains roughly similar numbers of examples for each class.
A varied dataset includes realistic differences in lighting, angle, distance and background.
More examples are not automatically better if they all repeat the same accidental pattern.
study.example: Twenty cup photos from one angle on one desk can teach less than twenty varied cup photos across different angles and backgrounds.

sessions.title: Break it and log the evidence
sessions.intro: Your goal is to find failures, not to make the model look good.

study.title: Testing and accuracy
body: Useful testing uses unseen examples: different objects, new angles, unusual lighting, cluttered backgrounds or partial views.
Accuracy is correct predictions divided by total predictions. It is useful, but it does not explain which kinds of errors occurred.
A model that never fails in your tests may simply mean the tests are too easy.
study.example: 8 correct predictions out of 10 tests gives 80% accuracy. The two failures are evidence worth investigating.

activity.instructions: Record at least 10 tests: actual class, prediction and an observation about angle, light, background or another condition.

sessions.title: Read the confusion matrix
sessions.intro: Accuracy hides which mistakes happened. The confusion matrix separates them.

study.title: Which error matters?
body: A confusion matrix compares what was actually true with what the model predicted.
Correct predictions sit where actual and predicted classes match; the other cells show the two directions of error.
Which error matters more depends on the job. The consequences of a spam-filter mistake and a medical-screening mistake are not the same.
study.example: Two models can have the same overall accuracy but make different kinds of mistakes, so the matrix can reveal a weakness that accuracy hides.

sessions.title: The shortcut experiment
sessions.intro: Deliberately build a flawed dataset so you can see shortcut learning happen.

study.title: Shortcut learning and bias
body: A model searches for statistical patterns that reduce error. It does not automatically know which pattern humans intended it to learn.
Shortcut learning happens when the model relies on an easy accidental clue, such as background colour, instead of the object itself.
Bias can enter through data even when nobody deliberately writes an unfair rule.
study.example: If cups are almost always photographed on a light background and bottles on a dark one, the model may learn background colour. Swap backgrounds and the prediction can collapse.

sessions.title: Improve model v2
sessions.intro: Use the failure evidence to make targeted changes, then test again fairly.

study.title: Improve with evidence
body: Propose changes that address the failure you actually observed: more variety, better balance, mixed backgrounds, clearer labels or additional representative examples.
Where possible, retest v2 using the same test set as v1 so the comparison is fair.
A better model is supported by before-and-after evidence, not by confidence or a single successful example.
study.example: If dark backgrounds caused cup errors, add both classes on light and dark backgrounds, retrain, then repeat the same background challenge.

study.title: A trustworthy evaluation is more than one score
body: Present what changed from v1 to v2, what improved, and what remains uncertain.
A confusion matrix shows error types that overall accuracy can hide.
Variety and balance can matter more than simply collecting a larger volume of near-identical examples.

blocks.title: Data Detective
blocks.description: Data is the raw material of AI. This chapter is an investigation: what does a service actually collect, what does it work out about you without you telling it, and who gets left out when a dataset is built?
blocks.mission: Audit one digital service at category level, then design a Responsible Data Card for it: what is collected, why, what is inferred, the risks, what controls users have, and what should not be collected at all.
route: Discover: your rights and the safeguards
blocks.final: Your data category audit of one service, your Responsible Data Card (Sheet A5), your dataset fairness redesign: before and after, and your reflection.

sessions.title: Data trail warm-up
sessions.intro: Pick a music, video or maps service. List what it can know directly and what it could work out, then sort your list into three piles.

study.title: Volunteered, observed, inferred
body: Personal data is any information about a person who could be identified from it. A service collects it in three ways, and the difference matters. Volunteered data is information you give on purpose: you typed it in or chose it. Your name, a playlist name, a “like”, a search.

Observed data is information recorded while you use something. Nobody asked you for it and you probably never saw it happen: how long you watched, where you were, what you skipped. Because it is collected quietly, most people never check whether it is accurate.

Inferred data is information a system guesses about you from the other two: your mood, your age range, what you'll buy, who you know. It was never given and never directly seen. It is a prediction about a person, and predictions can be wrong, unfair, or both.
study.example: A music app knows the playlist name you typed (volunteered), notices you skip every slow track after 11 pm (observed), and guesses you are a teenager who is often awake late (inferred). Only the first one is something you actually said.

sessions.title: Data Tracking Sherlock
sessions.intro: Choose one familiar service. Using its privacy policy or app-store listing, find the categories of data it says it collects.

study.title: Read the policy like a detective
body: Every service has to say somewhere what personal data it collects. That is usually a privacy policy, or the data list on its app-store page. Nobody reads them cover to cover, so read them the way a detective would: skim for the list of categories (“location”, “contacts”, “viewing history”) and ignore the legal filler.

Note anything surprising: a category you would not expect that service to need. Then note anything vague. “To improve our services” covers a lot; so does “partners” and “personalisation”. Vague words are where tracking hides, because they let the service follow what you do across pages, apps and time without ever saying so plainly.

Stay at category level. You are looking for the pattern of what kinds of data a service takes, not for anyone's private details. A good audit names the categories, marks the surprising ones, and quotes the vague ones so you can ask the “why collect it?” question next.
study.example: A maps app lists: precise location, search history, contacts (optional), device identifiers, and “usage information to improve our services”. Contacts is surprising for a map. “Usage information” is vague: it could mean anything from how often you open the app to every place you looked at.

sessions.title: Why collect it?
sessions.intro: For five data categories you found, complete the chain: COLLECTION → PURPOSE → USER BENEFIT → POSSIBLE RISK.

study.title: Purpose, benefit, risk
body: Data minimisation means collecting only what's genuinely needed for a stated purpose. So the first question for every category is: what is the purpose? A maps app that collects your location has an obvious one. A maps app that collects your contacts needs to explain itself.

Then ask who benefits. Some collection is genuinely useful to you: your listening history makes recommendations better, your location makes directions possible. Some collection mostly benefits the service or its advertisers, and you get little or nothing back. Be fair in both directions.

Finally ask what could go wrong. Data can leak, be sold, be combined with other data to identify you, or be used to infer things you never said. The risk of a category is not only what it is, but what it can be turned into: a year of location history is a map of where you live, study and sleep.
study.example: Location → to give directions → you get to the right place → a year of location history reveals your home, your school and your routine if it leaks. The purpose is real and the benefit is real; the risk is still worth writing down.

sessions.title: Cookies, scraping and the fairness challenge
sessions.intro: See how cookies, tracking and web scraping work, then take a flawed dataset for a school club-recommendation system and ask the hard question: who is missing?

study.title: Public is not the same as free to use
body: Cookies are small files a website stores on your device to remember or track you. Remembering is useful: you stay logged in, your basket survives. Tracking is following what you do across pages, apps or time, and the same cookie can do both. Web scraping is automatically copying data from public web pages, and it is how many datasets are built.

Public / private data is about whether data is openly available or restricted, and “public” doesn't mean “free to use for anything”. If something is publicly visible, is every reuse of it reasonable? A photo posted for friends is public. Is training a face-recognition model on it fair? The person made it visible for one purpose; scraping gives it another.

Now the dataset fairness challenge. Your scenario is an AI system for school club recommendations, built on the sign-up data below. Representativeness is whether a dataset actually reflects all the people it will affect. Decide what data you'd collect, then ask: who is missing? Students who joined mid-year? People without smartphones? Those who work nights? A dataset can be full of errors, but the quietest flaw is the people who are not in it at all.
study.example: Finding: column signup_date, Inconsistent format, "three date styles in one column (2026-09-07, 03/09/2026, 4 Sept 2026), so sorting by date would be wrong". That is a target, an issue type and a note someone else could check. Now ask the harder one yourself: which club has almost no rows from a whole year group or gender, and who does that leave out?

sessions.title: Your rights and the safeguards
sessions.intro: GDPR gives you rights. The EU AI Act adds a second idea. You don't need the legal detail; you need the instinct.

study.title: Discover: your rights and the safeguards
body: GDPR is the EU's data protection law; it gives people rights over their data. The principles that matter most for you: data should be collected for a clear purpose; only what's needed (minimisation); kept accurate and secure; used transparently; and you have rights to see it, correct it and sometimes delete it.

Consent means agreeing to a use of your data, freely and with real understanding. Consent buried in 40 pages nobody reads isn't real consent, and even genuine consent doesn't make a harmful or unfair use acceptable. So when a service says “you agreed”, the detective's question is still: to what, and was it needed?

The EU AI Act is an EU law that regulates AI by how risky its use is. The riskier the use of AI (say, deciding who gets a job), the stricter the rules. A playlist recommender is low risk. A system that decides who gets shortlisted, or which students get a place, is not, and it needs a person able to review, override or stop it.
study.example: A club-recommendation system suggests clubs to students: low stakes if it is only a suggestion. If the same system quietly decides who is “not club material” from a notes column, the stakes are higher, and so the rules should be stricter.

sessions.title: Design a better data plan
sessions.intro: Go back to your scenario. Remove fields you don't need, add a check for who's represented, decide how long data is kept, and mark the decisions that must have a human reviewing them. Then write your Responsible Data Card.

study.title: A better data plan, then the card
body: A better data plan starts by removing fields you don't need. If the purpose is recommending clubs, an inferred income band, a home Eircode and free-text opinions about students do not serve it; take them out before anyone trains anything. Then add a check for who's represented: compare the rows you have with the students the system will affect, and name the groups that are thin or absent.

Decide how long data is kept. Sign-up data for this year's clubs has no reason to exist in five years. Retention is part of minimisation: data you no longer hold cannot leak, be reused or be inferred from. Then mark the decisions that must have a human reviewing them before anything happens to a person: a recommendation can be automatic, a refusal or a ranking should not be.

The Responsible Data Card (Sheet A5) is where the whole investigation lands: what is collected, what is observed rather than typed, what might be inferred, why it is needed, what could go wrong, who might be missing or misrepresented, what should be removed or minimised, and what needs human review. Write it so that someone who never saw the data would still understand its limits.
study.example: Job shortlisting, before: the app collects home address, date of birth, a photo, school name, a "likely reliability" score inferred from social media, and keeps everything for ten years. After: name, contact email and the answers to three job-relevant questions only; a check each round that shortlisted candidates are not all from two schools; deleted three months after the role is filled; every rejection reviewed by a person before it is sent.

myths: If data is public, any use of it is ethical.
Public means visible. It doesn't mean the person agreed to every possible reuse. Context matters.
Anonymous data can never cause harm.
Combine a few “anonymous” facts (postcode, age, school) and you can often identify a person. And group-level data can still be used unfairly against a whole group.
Consent makes any data use OK.
Consent buried in 40 pages nobody reads isn't real consent. And even genuine consent doesn't make a harmful or unfair use acceptable.

sessions.title: Same task, different prompts
sessions.intro: Ask the AI one deliberately weak question, then ask it again. Compare what came back before you learn anything about prompting.

study.title: Same question, different answers
body: Generative AI is AI that creates new text, images, audio or code from learned patterns. A chatbot is the text version: you type a prompt, the instructions and context you give it, and it produces an answer that reads smoothly. Smooth is the problem. The wording sounds the same whether the content is right, half-right or invented.

So the first experiment is not about getting a good answer. It is about noticing. Everyone asks the same weak question, then asks it again or in a second model, and compares. Some parts will be the same every time; those are the patterns the model has seen most often. Some parts will change between runs for no reason you gave it; those were never checked facts to begin with.

Keep three lists as you read: what varied, what was missing, and what sounded confident with nothing behind it. A sentence that would need a source to be believed, but comes with none, is your first sight of hallucination: a fluent, confident output that's wrong or made up. You will check claims like that properly in the verification challenge later.
study.example: Ask “Tell me about the River Shannon.” twice. Both answers say it is Ireland's longest river. One says it is about 360 km long, the other says nearly 500 km. Same confident tone; at least one is wrong, and nothing in either answer tells you which.

sessions.title: What an LLM actually does
sessions.intro: Before you improve a single prompt, get the mental model right: what is the machine actually doing when it answers you?

study.title: Discover: what an LLM actually does
body: A large language model (LLM) is a generative model trained on huge amounts of text to predict and produce language. It has read an enormous amount of text and learned to predict what usually comes next. When you ask a question, it generates a likely continuation. That's why it's fluent.

It's also why it's not a database of checked facts. Pattern prediction is the LLM's basic move: predict what most likely comes next, word by word. Nothing in that move looks anything up, and nothing in it knows whether the sentence it just produced is true. It can produce a smooth, confident paragraph about something that never happened.

Confident wording is not confident truth. Keep that sentence. You'll need it. When the model is right, it is because the pattern it followed happened to match the world; when it is wrong, the wording gives you no warning. That is what hallucination means, and it is why anything you rely on has to be checked somewhere other than the chatbot.
study.example: Ask for the opening year of a power station and the model produces a plausible four-digit year in a confident sentence. It is not reading a record; it is continuing a pattern. The year might be right. The sentence would look identical if it were wrong.

sessions.title: Prompt Lab 1: C-T-C-F
sessions.intro: Take one weak prompt and rebuild it with four parts. Save the before and after outputs side by side. That's your v1 and v2.

study.title: Context, Task, Constraints, Format
body: Context is the background the model needs: who you are, what this is for, what you already know. Without it the model guesses an audience and a purpose, and it usually guesses the most average one. Task is the one clear thing you want it to do. One verb. “Tell me about” is not a task; “list”, “compare”, “explain” and “draft” are.

Constraints are the limits you set: length, level, what to avoid, what must be included. A constraint is how you stop the answer sprawling and how you make the model say “unsure” instead of inventing. Output format is the shape you want the answer in: a table, bullets, three options, questions first. Format decides whether you can actually use what comes back.

Rebuild your weak prompt with all four parts, run the original (v1) and the rebuilt version (v2) in the same tool, and save both outputs. Record what you changed and what the output did differently. Then the honest question: was it better, and why? Some of the change is your prompt. Some is just the model varying between runs. Telling those apart is the whole skill.
study.example: v1: “Tell me about the River Shannon.” v2: “I am a Transition Year student preparing a two-minute talk for my class (context). List the five most important facts about the River Shannon (task). Under 120 words, plain language, and write ‘unsure’ next to any figure you are not certain of (constraints). Numbered list, one fact per line (format).”

sessions.title: Prompt Lab 2: iterate
sessions.intro: Now try adding one thing at a time and compare each version. Which additions actually helped, and which just made the prompt longer?

study.title: One change per round
body: Iteration is improving in rounds, comparing each version. The rule for this lab is one change per round. If you add three things at once and the answer improves, you have no idea which of the three did it, and next time you will add all three again out of superstition.

Four additions are worth trying, one at a time: an example of what good looks like; the audience; success criteria, meaning how you will judge the answer; or “ask me questions before you answer”. Each changes something different. An example shapes the style, the audience shapes the level, success criteria shape what the model prioritises, and asking questions first surfaces the context you forgot to give.

Keep the constraints and format from v2 while you test additions, so the comparison is fair. When you have found the additions that genuinely helped, write your v3: tested and revised. A longer prompt that produced the same answer is not a better prompt. Clear beats long.
study.example: Adding “the audience is 15-year-olds who have never seen the river” changed the vocabulary and cut the jargon. Adding “be as detailed as possible” doubled the length and added two more unchecked figures. One helped; one just made the prompt longer.

sessions.title: Four useful roles
sessions.intro: Try the AI in four different jobs. Each has a different prompt style and a different risk.

study.title: Tutor, brainstorm partner, critic, transformer
body: Tutor: “Explain X to me, then quiz me.” The prompt sets up a loop: an explanation, then questions back to you. Risk: it explains something wrong, fluently, and then quizzes you on the wrong thing. Brainstorm partner: “Give me 10 unusual angles on X.” Good for getting unstuck. Risk: you stop generating your own, and every idea starts sounding like the model's.

Critic: “Here's my draft. What's weak?” You give it your own work and ask for problems. Risk: it's too polite, or invents problems so that it has something to say. Transformer: “Turn this into a table / a summary / simpler language.” You give it text and ask for a different shape. Risk: it drops or changes meaning while making it look tidier.

Run each role once. For each, record the prompt, what it did well, and the risk you actually saw, not only the one the book warned you about. Use a made-up draft or a topic from this chapter, never personal writing about yourself or anyone else. The roles where the AI helps you think are usually more useful than the ones where it thinks for you.
study.example: As a transformer, the model turned a paragraph about Ardnacrusha into a neat three-row table and quietly changed “completed in 1929” to “opened in the 1920s”. Tidier, and less precise. That is the transformer risk in one row.

sessions.title: Verification challenge
sessions.intro: Ask the AI about a topic with several checkable facts. Then pick three claims and verify each one yourself using reliable sources. Record it on Sheet A2.

study.title: Supported, uncertain or wrong
body: Verification is checking a claim against independent, reliable evidence. Independent means not the chatbot, and not a page that copied the chatbot. Reliable is about source quality: how trustworthy a source is: who made it, why, and how it can be checked. An official record, a national body, a museum, a peer-reviewed paper or a primary document beats a blog, a forum answer or a page with no author.

Pick a topic from the download, ask the AI about it, and choose three claims that would matter if wrong: figures, dates, names, causes. For each one find a source, note its name and where you found it, and give a verdict. Supported: a reliable source says the same. Uncertain: sources disagree, or you found nothing either way. Wrong: a reliable source contradicts it.

The last column is the one people skip: what you changed because of the check. A wrong claim comes out of your talk. An uncertain one gets a hedge or a question mark. A supported one gets its source written next to it. If the AI gave you a citation, check that too. LLMs generate citations the same way they generate everything else: by pattern.
study.example: Claim: “Lough Derg is the largest lake in Ireland.” Source: Tailte Éireann lake data and Waterways Ireland. Verdict: wrong. It is the largest lake on the Shannon, but Lough Neagh is far larger. What I changed: reworded the sentence to what the source supports and wrote the source next to it. That row is Sheet A2 done properly.

sessions.title: Injecting doubt
sessions.intro: Ask the model leading questions on purpose and watch how the framing of your question shapes the answer.

study.title: The question that answers itself
body: “Why is X better than Y?” already contains an answer: X is better, please justify it. A pattern-predictor that has read millions of persuasive articles will oblige. “Compare X and Y” contains no answer, so the most likely continuation is a balanced comparison. Same topic, same model, and the framing of the question decides what you get.

This is confirmation bias: the habit of looking for evidence that agrees with what you already think. The model will happily feed yours. It is not lying and it is not agreeing with you on purpose; it is continuing the pattern your question started. That makes leading questions the fastest way to get a confident answer that only sounds like evidence.

Run the pair. Ask a leading version and a neutral version of the same question, keep everything else identical, and record how the two answers differ. Then write down what this means for your own responsibility: if the framing is yours, the bias in the answer is yours too. A prompt that is fair to both sides is also the prompt that is safer for the other people who will read the output.
study.example: “Why is wind power better than solar in Ireland?” produced four reasons for wind and none against. “Compare wind and solar power in Ireland” produced two columns with costs and drawbacks for each. Only the second could be used honestly in a talk.

study.title: A template with placeholders
body: A template is a prompt with the parts that change taken out and replaced by [placeholders]. The four parts are the same as Lab 1: context, task, constraints, output format. What makes it reusable is that the constraints and format stay fixed while the topic and audience swap in, so every run is comparable with the last.

Pick a task you genuinely have. Write the template, then explain why each part is there. If you cannot say what a line does, it is probably one of the additions from Lab 2 that just made the prompt longer, and it should go.

Finish with the honest section: when you would use it again, and what you would still check by hand. A good template includes its own verification step, something like “mark any figure or name you are not sure of”, because iteration can make the answer more useful, but it cannot turn a pattern-predictor into a fact-checker.

sessions.title: Red-team a prompt

study.title: One ambiguity, one missing constraint, one claim to check
body: Red-teaming means attacking your own work before someone else does. For a prompt, three things go wrong most often. An ambiguity: a word or phrase the model could read two ways, so the answer might be about the wrong thing. A missing constraint: no length, level, date range or “say if unsure”, so the model fills the gap with its most average guess.

The third is a claim that would need checking: something the prompt invites the model to state as fact, such as a year, a statistic or a quotation, with no instruction to source it. Those are the sentences most likely to be hallucinated, and they are also the ones most likely to be copied straight into someone's work without anyone judging the source quality.

Run the prompt if you can, but you can red-team it on paper too. Read it the way the model would: what is the most likely continuation, and where would a fluent wrong answer slip in? Write one of each, give the notes back if it was a partner's, and keep a copy: you will want the same three checks for your own template.
study.example: “Write about the history of our town and include the year it was founded.” Ambiguity: which town? Missing constraint: how long, and for whom? Claim to check: the founding year, which the model will supply confidently whether or not any record exists.

sessions.title: The confidence trap
sessions.intro: You'll see three confident statements. One is true, one is false, one can't be verified either way. Rank how confident you are in each before checking. Then check. Notice which one fooled you and why.

study.title: Confident is not the same as correct
body: All three statements on the claim cards are written in the same confident tone. That is the trap. Misinformation is false or misleading information, spread without meaning harm; disinformation is false information spread on purpose to deceive. Both arrive sounding just as sure of themselves as the truth does, and an AI hallucination, a fluent but wrong or invented output, sounds exactly the same again.

So before you check anything, write down how confident you are in each statement, from 1 to 5. That number is the experiment. When you check, the statements will not all land the same way: some can be settled against a source, and at least one cannot be settled either way because nobody has measured it. Notice which one your confidence got wrong and what it was reacting to: a familiar-sounding fact, a precise year, a tidy round number.

Trusting a machine's output more than you should, just because it's a machine, is called automation bias, and it works on people too: a confident person, a tidy paragraph, a number with a decimal point. The habit this chapter builds is to treat confidence as a feeling to notice, not as evidence. Evidence comes from checking, which is what the rest of the chapter is about.
study.example: “Ireland has the youngest population in the European Union.” It sounds right, because you have heard something like it before and it flatters the place you live. A one-tab check against Eurostat's median-age table is enough to settle it either way, and until you have run that check your confidence is only familiarity. None of the three cards is this claim; work them the same way.

study.title: Stop, Investigate, Find, Trace
body: Stop. Don't share or react yet. Notice how it makes you feel. A post that makes you angry or thrilled is doing something to you before you have checked a single word, and that feeling is often the point of the framing: the wording and emphasis chosen to shape what a message makes you feel or believe. Stopping costs nothing and it is the habit that makes the other three possible.

Investigate the source. Who made this? Why? What do others say about them? That is provenance: where something came from and how it got to you. Find better coverage. Open new tabs. Do reliable, independent sources agree? Leaving the page you are on to see what other sources say about it is lateral reading, and it is how professional fact-checkers work: sideways, in new tabs, not by scrolling further down the same page.

Trace the claim. Follow it back to the original evidence. Was context lost? A statistic, a quote or a headline can pass through ten sites and change a little each time, and the version that reaches you may say something the original never did. The four habits go in this order because each one is cheaper than the next: stopping takes a second, tracing a claim can take ten minutes, and you only need to trace the claims that survived the first three checks.
study.example: A headline says “Study finds phones halve teenagers' attention span.” Stop: it made you nod. Investigate the source: a site you have never heard of with no author. Find better coverage: two newspapers ran it, both citing the same site. Trace the claim: the study measured 40 students for one afternoon and never used the word “halve”. Ten minutes, four habits, one claim that shrank at every step.

sessions.title: AI News Detective
sessions.intro: Go through a short news-style article written in the style of AI with a highlighter. Mark: factual claims, emotional framing, missing sources, and certainty that isn't backed up. Count them.

study.title: Four colours of highlighter
body: The article in this session was written for the course in the style of AI-generated news and is labelled as synthetic at the top; no real plan, law, survey or report is described. Read it the way a good journalist reads a press release: sentence by sentence, asking what each sentence is doing. Four things are worth marking. A factual claim is a sentence that could be checked: a year, a number, a name, a statement that something exists. Emotional framing is wording chosen to make you feel something before you have checked anything.

A missing source is a claim that would need one and comes without it: “a recent survey”, “experts”, “the report”, with no name, date or link. Unsupported certainty is a sentence that is sure of itself with nothing behind it: “It is beyond doubt”, “Experts agree”, “will”. A sentence can earn more than one mark, and the most misleading sentences usually do: a confident, emotional, unsourced claim is the AI hallucination in its natural habitat.

Mark at least six sentences, use at least three of the four types, and write a short note on each one saying what you noticed. Then count them, as the book says. The count tells you what kind of article this is: mostly checkable claims with sources, or mostly feeling and certainty with nothing underneath. You will verify the factual claims in the next session, so the more carefully you mark them now, the easier that becomes.
study.example: “It is beyond doubt that students who refuse to use them will be left behind.” Unsupported certainty: nothing backs “beyond doubt”. Emotional framing: “refuse” and “left behind” are chosen to worry you. No factual claim at all: there is nothing in the sentence you could check. Two marks, one note: sounds like a fact, is actually a feeling.

study.title: Sideways, in new tabs
body: Lateral reading means checking a source by leaving it and seeing what other sources say about it. For each factual claim you marked, open a new tab and search for the claim itself, not the article. Look for a source that is independent of the original: an official body, a national statistics office, a law database, a museum, a primary document. A page that repeats the article's wording, or cites the article, is not independent; it is the same claim wearing a different address.

Do not fact-check by asking another chatbot. That's just asking a second pattern-predictor. A chatbot will produce a confident answer about the “National AI Tutoring Act 2025” whether or not it exists, because it is continuing a pattern, not reading a record. Provenance is where something came from and how it got to you, and a chatbot's answer has no provenance you can follow.

Give each claim a verdict. Supported: an independent, reliable source says the same. Uncertain: sources disagree, the claim is too vague to check, or you found nothing either way. Wrong: a reliable source contradicts it, or the thing it names does not exist. Write down where you looked even when you found nothing; “no such Act on the Irish Statute Book” is a finding, and it is the finding that separates checking from believing.
study.example: Claim: “Transition Year was founded in 1986.” New tab: the Department of Education and the NCCA both give 1974 as the pilot year in three schools, and 1994 as the year it was made widely available. Independent of the article: yes, official records. Verdict: wrong. Note the two dates; the article's year matches neither.

sessions.title: Bias simulator
sessions.intro: Build a biased outcome on purpose, then try to fix it. Change how much of one group is in the training data, decide whether the model can see a sensitive field, and watch what happens to each group.

study.title: Where bias gets in
body: Bias is a systematic skew in data, design or use that produces unfair results, and it can get in at every stage of a system's life. Before the data exists, past decisions may already have been unequal, so the history the model learns from is skewed. At collection, only some people end up in the dataset: selection bias, when the data collected doesn't fairly represent the whole picture, and representation bias, when some groups are missing or under-counted. At labelling, the people writing the answers may apply a label differently for different groups.

Then there is feature choice: a field like postcode can stand in for a group even after the sensitive field has been removed, which is called a proxy. In training, the model learns the patterns of the majority group best. In evaluation, the test set may hide the hard cases. In deployment, the model may be used for something it was never tested on. And in how a person trusts the output, automation bias: the person believes the machine because it looks objective. Removing one field fixes none of the other stages.

One number can hide all of this. A model gets 18 out of 20 decisions right for Group A (90%) and 11 out of 20 right for Group B (55%). Reported as a single figure, it scores 29 out of 40, or 72.5%. That sounds like a passable system. It is a system that fails one group nearly half the time. In the simulator you will see the same thing happen: the overall number moves a little while one group moves a lot, and the fix that looks obvious, deleting the sensitive field, helps only as much as the proxy is weak.
study.example: Set Group B to 10% of the training data and keep the sensitive field: Group A stays at 18/20 while Group B falls to 2/20, and the overall figure still reads 50%. Now remove the field with the postcode proxy at 80%: Group B rises, but not to where Group A is, because the postcode is still telling the model most of what the field did.

sessions.title: Bias stations
sessions.intro: Four short scenarios, four stations: hiring data, image generation and stereotypes, school discipline analytics, recommendation feeds. At each one, ask: where could bias enter (the data? the design? how people use it?) and who would be affected?

study.title: Four stations, three doors
body: Every station is the same three questions. Where could bias enter: in the data, in the design, or in how people use it? Who would be affected? And which kind of bias is it? Selection bias, when the data collected doesn't fairly represent the whole picture. Representation bias, when some groups are missing or under-counted. Framing, when the wording and emphasis shape what a person believes about the output. Automation bias, when the people using the system trust it more than they should, just because it's a machine. And a proxy, when a harmless-looking field stands in for a sensitive one.

Hiring data: a model trained on who was hired before learns who was hired before, including every reason that had nothing to do with doing the job well. Image generation and stereotypes: a model trained on the internet's pictures produces the internet's assumptions about who does which job. The discipline analytics card is the book's school scenario, run here as a training centre: a model that predicts who is “likely to cause trouble” from past records learns who was written up before, not who did what.

Recommendation feeds: a feed that learns from what you click shows you more of it, and the design decides whether “more of it” means more variety or more of the same. At each station, name the mechanism and the person on the receiving end. The mechanism matters because it decides the fix: a representation problem needs different data, a proxy problem needs a different design, and an automation problem needs a different rule about how people use the output.
study.example: A worked example on a fifth scenario, not on the cards: a model that scores loan applications. Where it enters: in the data, because past lending decisions are the decisions the previous staff made, and in the design, because “years at the same address” looks neutral and stands in for how settled and how well-off an applicant is. Who is affected: applicants who move often, who are refused for something that has nothing to do with repaying. Kind: a proxy in the design, and automation bias in the staff who read the score as an answer. Work each station the same way, in your own words.

sessions.title: Improve the output
sessions.intro: Rewrite the article. Keep only the verified claims. Label anything uncertain as uncertain. Add real sources. Take out the loaded framing. Your version should be less exciting and more trustworthy. That's the point.

study.title: Less exciting, more trustworthy
body: You now have three lists from your own work: the claims your verification table marked supported, the ones it marked uncertain, and the ones it marked wrong. The corrected version is built from the first list, with the second list kept but labelled, and the third list gone. Next to every claim you keep, write the real source you found. A claim with a source is worth more than five without, however dull it reads.

Then take out the loaded framing. “Drowning in an outdated system” becomes nothing, because it was never a claim. “Experts agree” becomes either a named expert who actually said it, or nothing. Certainty that nothing backed becomes the honest version: “no plan has been announced”, “one survey with no published method”. That is what labelling uncertainty as uncertain looks like in practice.

Your version should be less exciting and more trustworthy. That's the point. Misinformation spreads because it is more interesting than the truth, and a hallucination is interesting for the same reason: it says what a pattern predicts people want to read. Read your corrected version back and ask the honest question: could a sentence in it still be accurate and still be misleading, because of what it leaves out or how it is ordered? If so, fix that too.
study.example: Original: “The National AI Tutoring Act 2025 makes the rollout a legal requirement for every school in the country.” Corrected: removed; no such Act exists on the Irish Statute Book (irishstatutebook.ie, searched by title). Original: “A recent survey found that 78% of parents want an AI tutor in their child's classroom.” Corrected: “One unnamed survey is reported to have found 78% support; the survey, its method and its sample size could not be found, so this figure is uncertain.”

sessions.title: Synthetic media

study.title: Seeing is not checking
body: Synthetic media, or a deepfake, is AI-generated audio, image or video that looks real. A voice can be cloned from a short recording, a face can be placed into a scene, and a clip can be produced of an event that never happened. None of this needs special skill any more, and the polished result is no sign of anything: looking professional now costs nothing.

The habit is the same one you used on the article, applied to a clip. Stop, and notice that it made you angry; that is the feeling disinformation is designed to produce, because angry people share. Investigate the source: who posted it, and where did it come from before that? Provenance is the whole question with synthetic media. Find better coverage: has anyone independent reported the same event, or is every copy of the clip pointing back at one account?

Ask who gains if you share it, look for the original rather than a re-upload, and wait. A real event has more than one witness and more than one source; a clip that exists only as itself is a clip you cannot verify. The checklist download puts these habits in one place. Nothing here needs a scary example; it needs the same four habits, used before the clip has finished playing.
study.example: A clip of a well-known person saying something outrageous appears in a group chat. Stop: it made you furious. Investigate: the account that posted it was created last week. Find better coverage: no news outlet has it, and every copy online links back to that account. Provenance: none. Verdict: not something you can share as true, whatever it looks like.

sessions.title: Reflection: my three-step rule
sessions.intro: Write your own three-step rule for checking important AI-generated information. Make it short enough to actually use.

study.title: Three steps you will actually take
body: You have ranked your confidence and been fooled, marked up an article, checked its claims sideways in new tabs, built a biased model and tried to fix it, and rewritten something misleading into something dull and true. Every one of those used the same few moves: stop, look at where it came from, look for an independent source, trace the claim, and treat confidence as a feeling rather than evidence.

Your rule is three of those moves, in the order you would really do them, written short enough to say to yourself in the moment before you share, repeat or rely on something. A rule with seven steps is a rule nobody uses. A rule that says “check it” is a rule that tells you nothing. Somewhere between is a rule with three verbs and three objects: what you do, to what.

Your portfolio for this chapter is your annotated AI output, your verification table, your bias analysis from the stations and the simulator, your corrected version, and this rule. Check that each one exists before you move on. Lateral reading and provenance are the two words most likely to end up in your rule; automation bias is the reason you need one.

study.title: Audience and expectations
body: Disclosure says clearly when and how AI helped. What an audience needs depends on the purpose of the work and what they expect from its author.
Private brainstorming and assessed work have different expectations. When the expectations are unclear, check with the training centre or intended audience before relying on an assumption.
A useful disclosure names the assistance and your responsibility. People can disagree reasonably about how much detail an audience needs; explain the expectation behind your choice.
study.example: For a club poster, a designer might explain that AI suggested headings while the club checked dates and wrote the final text.

body: A learning contract is your own set of rules for when AI helps and where you retain responsibility. Make each rule observable.
A repeatable workflow has checkpoints: someone verifies the evidence, someone decides what to keep, and someone approves before it is used.
Keep enough evidence to explain what you tried, what changed and what you can now explain. Disclosure should fit the audience and the expectations for your assessed work.
